title: What are your thoughts on why Werner Herzog's "Aguirre, The Wrath of God" is so captivating all these years later?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

The production of this film is insane, just imaging how they made the film as you watch it is reason enough to watch it I think. If you read about Klaus Kinski, you'll see he's a pretty insane and controversial guy to say the least, and that translates to a very captivating screen presence. The dude has no limits.

As for your question on these characters, I'd say it's probably some kind of unconscious desire to explore the darkest places in our mind that we aren't allowed to go in the world. Anything normal people shouldn't do, stealing, killing, etc has a certain mystique and intrigue to it, so it's intoxicating to live vicariously through characters that are allowed to live their lives in such a subversive way.

There's a deep part of the human physique that is attracted power, but we're civilized so we keep that in balance with everything else. It's fun to watch characters tip the scales in one way completely.
Just wanted to add- watch “My Best Fiend” for some more great context on Herzog, Kinski and Aguirre.

Absolutely. I watched it while researching the video essay. Helped a lot with framing Kinski's approach to acting, especially Aguirre. Herzog also speaks about his fascination with Kinski from his childhood when they both happened to live in the same flat in post-war Germany.

Because it's a story about obsessive madness, starring an actual unhinged mad-man, directed by an actual ambitious mad-man. It's unique and exists only because Herzog is somehow competent and strategic in harnessing his own madness and capturing his vision.


It's Herzog's 'thing'. You're watching  documentary footage of an insanely realised scenario at the same time as following a fictional narrative. Because of the very real madness at play there's this feeling that anything could happen. I love it.

Aesthetically, I find the use of the score incredibly enduring. The earthy, turbulent physicality of the imagery is perfectly offset by the serene, celestial music - it's much more powerful than simple comic juxtaposition, it's rapturous. Maybe there *is* a wrathful god here. These sequences being the bookends of the movie are part of why Aguirre leaves such a lasting impression.

In terms of budget vs. quality,  this is the best movie of all time.

Incredibly eloquent,  almost minimalist in its approach, every shot is a true conquest by a master of the craft. 

Few movies are a perfect ten, but even fewer are a perfect 11.

It's one of my all time favorite movies, there is something truly haunting about it. Its the only movie I've seen where I actually feel the danger the cast is put in to film this.

Roger Ebert wrote about it extensively over the years as it was one of his top 10 movies.  All of his essays and reviews on it are worth checking out.

One of my favourite movies. It's like a fever dream. You can feel the stifling heat and humidity, and the absurdity of europeans putting themselves through pathetic power squabbles in a place of abundant beauty. The final scenes are stunning, the Popol Vuh soundtrack a work of prog rock genius, the cinematography a masterclass. The boat in the tree is a wonderfully surreal moment. I think I'll go watch it right now.

It's a very powerful thing about art to talk about difficult aspects of human nature, manifest and latent, joyous and terrible, absurd or more minute. We all have nightmares, and I think difficult/violent/transgressive/blasphemous pieces can allow everyone involved (authors and readers) to reflect on them, in some way or another.      
    
Herzog's movies in particular have that "spiraling out of control into madness" tone down to a science. And he doesn't pull any punches, it's not like he's particularly interested in symbolism. He just shows you people going insane while attempting to do unreasonable things, or driven mad by their inability to cope with reality.       
            
And he can be quite operatic, but even a smaller piece like Heart of Glass retains those hallucinatory and haunting qualitirs. [As we all know, it's very easy to hypnotize a chicken.](https://youtu.be/QhMo4WlBmGM?si=-YB-cZHOOR8o6wn_) His documentary on the North Pole is also kinda eerie in a an interesting way.
Seen it countless times. Own it on DVD. Have the Doc. And Have the book! It’s my favorite of the Kinski/herzog films.

That's not Kinski's voice. The audio for the entire movie was recorded in post-production and Kinski was dubbed by Gerd Martienzen because Kinski demanded too much money for recording sessions.

Holy shit I never knew this! Consider my mind blown. Wow

Regardless! Watch it in German, all the English dubs always suck.

I'll also jump in to say that it is one of those films that just wouldn't be made today, or made like it was. To film a story about Spanish conquistadors travelling down the amazon on rafts, they got people in costumes to get on rafts and go down the amazon. The authenticity would have been diluted with CGI and water stages today.
If anything, though, it's due credit to Martienzen for pulling off such an accurate Kinski impression.
[Conquest of the Useless: Reflections from the Making of Fitzcarraldo](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/6004348-conquest-of-the-useless)

> haunting 

This is the word for it. The scene of the horse as they float away from it down the river is one that likes to wake me up at night sometimes.

It’s an epic and I think every film aficionado should watch it. Like someone else said, the production made it. Werzog and every person on location were against real life threats from not only nature but from their own—Klaus Kinski. Kinski was a psycho going after anyone who got in his way of his divine talents. Everything surrounding this film is crazy.

I love a couple of his films; Fitzcarraldo and above all Woyzeck, also with Kinski. But I really struggle to get into Aguirre; the opening scene is breathtaking and knowing about the shoot helps, but I cannot suspend my disbelief: it has a stilted quality which stops the natural flow of dialogue and movement (all IMO, of course). Maybe I'll try again at some point, but it didn't work for me. But that's life.
It definitely wouldn't be made today. Everything about this movie was pushing boundaries and being on the bleeding edge.

I just watched it for the first time, I mean this as a compliment, it feels unpolished and raw. The fact that  everything you see is in camera, and no after effects really make it amazing. The props were all built and were functional (to a degree), and the indigenous extras did a great job. Unfortunately since I bought the apple version I only have it in English, which is unfortunate since I can speak and understand German, and would have enjoyed the original dialogue. 

That said the dub is pretty good all things considered, and they were speaking modern German, not 16th century Spanish, so it is not as though it is a more authentic presentation. 

It reminds me with the film stock and the ratio of documentaries I used to watch in anthropology class, especially given the environment.

The movie was actually filmed in English, though - the cast and crew were from many different countries and English was the common tongue so they used that - you can clearly see the actors are speaking English words. It was dubbed into German in post-production , and then *again* into English for international distribution. It’s interesting to contemplate what should be considered the “original” language.

This film to me sort of is a microcosm of humanity, showcasing the futility and absurdity of our own organization, hierarchy, and pursuits. Watching these people, as presented in that cold and detached perspective, conduct themselves on that raft in total isolation is like watching the entirety of human history unfold all at once. They could easily reorganize and make a course correction, but they got swept up in their ways and were all eventually overcome by nature. I find watching this movie fascinating because once you zoom out of that microcosm film and apply it to reality, our own conclusion seems both inevitable and in our nature.

Really interesting video essay. Thank you, OP, I enjoyed this, especially how you put the movie and its themes in the historical context of Herzog’s life growing during up WWII. You had a lot of great insights here and really hit on what makes the film so engrossing. I also recently read an interesting article over at [Quilette](https://quillette.com/2024/03/28/werner-herzogs-new-memoir-jaspreet-singh-boparai/) about Herzog’s new memoir. I think you would find that intriguing as well, if you haven’t already read the memoir and/or the article. Thanks again for sharing your thoughts with us. I hope you will share other video essays with us in the future.

Once again, I'm fascinated by the timing of this thread popping up. I just watched this for the first time this week. A couple of things that immediately stood out to me about the film:

- Was struck by the eerie silence and eerily beautiful landscapes, which seemed to reverberate with the weight of human hubris and the search for gold. 

- The performances were phenomenal, particularly Klaus Kinski's portrayal of the titular Aguirre, whose descent into madness was, in a word, terrifying. 

- Herzog's direction was masterful... he weaved together the themes of obsession, morality, and the destructive power of unchecked ambition.

- Unforgettable ambient soundtrack that warranted multiple re-listens for me
Thanks so much for your kind words! It's my first video essay so what you wrote really means a lot. I haven't read Herzog's memoir yet, but thanks for the recommendation and article :)
